title: Sterile Hypopyon: The Inflammatory Deep Dive
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to the sterile accumulation of leukocytes in the anterior chamber. Differentiating non-infectious inflammatory responses from infectious endophthalmitis is critical for vision-saving management.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: A sterile hypopyon is the gravitational settling of inflammatory cells (predominantly polymorphonuclear leukocytes) in the inferior angle of the anterior chamber in the absence of an active microbial infection. It represents a severe breakdown of the blood-aqueous barrier and is a hallmark of intense intraocular inflammation, often associated with specific systemic HLA-B27 syndromes or toxic insults.

sections.title: The Great Divide: Sterile vs. Infectious
Ocular Examination Findings
content: Inferior layering of white cells (level measured in mm)
Ciliary flush / Circumcorneal injection
Fibrinous exudate in the pupil area
Posterior synechiae (PS) formation (Common in HLA-B27)
Corneal edema (Limbus-to-limbus in TASS)
Variable IOP (Low due to ciliary body shutdown or High due to trabeculitis)
Shifting hypopyon (Classic for Behçet's Disease)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: Step 1: Rule out infection via Vitreous/AC tap if post-op or post-injection.
Step 2: HLA-B27 genetic testing for systemic association.
Step 3: Chest X-ray or CT for Sarcoidosis (Bilateral hilar adenopathy).
Step 4: Syphilis serology (RPR/VDRL) and FTA-ABS.
Step 5: B-Scan ultrasound to assess posterior segment/vitritis.
Step 6: Serum ACE levels and Lysozyme.

sections.title: Toxic Anterior Segment Syndrome (TASS)
content: Acute sterile inflammation following intraocular surgery.
Causes: Denatured OVDs, detergents on instruments, contaminated solutions.
Onset: Characteristically 12–24 hours post-surgery.
Sign: Diffuse limbus-to-limbus corneal edema.
Treatment: Intensive topical steroids (Prednisolone Acetate 1% q1h).

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Suspect Infection
content: Pain out of proportion to clinical signs.
Rapidly progressive vitritis / loss of red reflex.
Hypopyon appearing >48 hours post-cataract surgery.
History of recent trauma with organic matter.
Lack of response to hourly topical steroids within 24 hours.

sections.title: Management & Treatment Protocol
content: 1. Aggressive Topical Steroids: Prednisolone Acetate 1% or Dexamethasone 0.1% every 1-2 hours initially.
2. Cycloplegia: Atropine 1% BID or Homatropine 5% TID to prevent posterior synechiae and reduce pain.
3. Subconjunctival Injections: Dexamethasone 4mg/1ml for severe cases.
4. Systemic Therapy: Oral Prednisone (1mg/kg/day) for bilateral or refractory cases.
5. Immunomodulators: Anti-TNF-alpha (Infliximab) specifically for Behçet disease.
6. Tapering: Slow taper over 4-6 weeks to prevent rebound inflammation.

content.explanation: B: Behçet's; A: Ankylosing Spondylitis; S: Sarcoidosis; H: HLA-B27 Associated (Psoriatic arthritis, IBD, Reactive arthritis).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The hypopyon of Behçet is 'cold' and 'mobile' (shifts with head tilt).
Always check for a hidden IOL haptic or lens fragment in chronic hypopyon.
Pseudo-hypopyon from Retinoblastoma is composed of tumor cells, not WBCs.
Intravitreal Triamcinolone can mimic a hypopyon (pseudohypopyon).

rows: CMV Retinitis treatment; often needs Probenecid.

sections.title: The HAWK & HARRIER Studies (Clinical context)
sections.content: Recent landmark studies identified an increased incidence of sterile intraocular inflammation (4.6%) and retinal vasculitis following Brolucizumab (Beovu) injections for nAMD. Clinicians must distinguish this from endophthalmitis to avoid unnecessary intravitreal antibiotics and focus on steroid therapy.

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
content: Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) - most common cause of vision loss.
Secondary Glaucoma due to peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS).
Complicated Cataract (Posterior subcapsular).
Phthisis Bulbi (in chronic/recurrent Behçet's).
